title: Regional Lean catheter project across four hospitals: protocol revision flags analysis and ethics, late audit reply refused
notes: Expert path on a multi-site Lean project. Seven fixture records are appraised into six claims; the decision (kind implementation) rests on c1, c2, c3, c4 and c6, with the council gate met and Hospital D's data sharing gate unknown, so it is accepted with the action blocked. Dependency closure across stages (G8): the first protocol reply ignores two investigator facts (one Lean coach, one hospital at a time; Hospital D on paper), Analysis and Ethics are drafted on it, then the investigator re-runs Protocol (call 2); both completed downstream stages are flagged for review, Analysis is redone (call 2) and leaves the list, and Ethics is re-reviewed and marked complete by hand, so the closure ends with needsReview empty. Late reply (G6): after an applied audit call (positive control), the investigator requests a re-audit and edits the audit notes while it is pending; the reply for audit call 2 must be refused with nothing applied. The format has no step for a pending request, so this scenario represents it as audit call 1, a set-field on audit.improvementNotes (the request is sent at that step, before the edit is saved) and audit call 2 as the late reply; the runner must send the request before executing the set-field and deliver the reply after it. Record ids are stableRecordId(record) imported from src/lib/evidence/records.ts in the author's generator: DOI-based for records 1, 3, 5, 7 (ev-1nyhpv9, ev-0abegw1, ev-1bdpaih, ev-03gnd4n) and titleYearKey-based for records 2, 4, 6 (ev-1s4dbl6, ev-0jtvr38, ev-107rvsr). Requires D27 (substantive audit content in studyRevision; at 875fe59 the audit object is excluded, so the late reply would overwrite the investigator's notes), S13 (appraisal), S11 (selectionStatus, actionStatus) and D5 (status text, review required). Catches: downstream stages left complete after an upstream revision, a flag that never clears after re-review, a late model reply overwriting investigator text, and a refused reply that still changes the store.

inputs.need:
I lead infection prevention and control for a regional health system with four acute hospitals (A to D) and 12 adult medical and surgical wards that we have agreed to work on first. Indwelling urinary catheters stay in too long. Our last quarterly point count found a catheter in 19 percent of ward patients, and when we reviewed 120 catheters, 38 had no documented indication on the day of review. Our catheter-associated urinary tract infection rate on these wards is about 2.3 per 1,000 catheter days, and two patients developed bacteraemia from a catheter source last year.

We want to run a Lean improvement project across the four hospitals. The idea is to value stream map the catheter pathway from insertion (mostly in emergency and theatres) to removal, find the waits and handoffs where catheters are forgotten, and then introduce standard work: a nurse-driven removal protocol, a daily catheter check at the morning huddle, and a removal reminder built into the nursing flowsheet. Each hospital has a ward manager champion, and the regional Lean office has one Lean coach who can support one hospital at a time, for about three months each.

What I need: a sensible primary measure (catheter days per 100 patient days, the proportion of catheters without a valid indication, or infections), a measurement set-up that can tell change from noise across four hospitals that start at different times, what the statistics should look like, how to handle the fact that one hospital's flowsheet cannot produce catheter days automatically, and what we need to do about ethics for a system-wide project. I also want to avoid claiming an infection effect we cannot detect with these numbers. The regional quality council has approved the project; Hospital D's information governance office has not yet agreed to share ward-level data.
inputs.constraints: No new funding. One Lean coach supports one hospital at a time for about three months. Measurement must use existing flowsheets and point counts; no chart review beyond 20 charts per ward per month.

response.title: Lean catheter pathway across four hospitals: catheter days and catheter-associated infections
response.subtitle: Lean project with staggered starts on 12 wards in Hospitals A to D
response.statement: Indwelling urinary catheters stay in longer than needed on 12 medical and surgical wards across four hospitals: 19 percent of ward patients had a catheter at the last point count and 38 of 120 reviewed catheters had no documented indication. The project will use value stream mapping and standard work (nurse-driven removal, a daily huddle check and a flowsheet reminder) to shorten catheter duration, measured in a way that separates real change from noise across hospitals that start at different times.
response.whoAffected: Adult inpatients on 12 wards, especially older men after surgery and patients catheterised in emergency or theatres; ward nurses who own removal; physicians and theatre teams who insert catheters; the four ward manager champions.
response.whatHurts: Unneeded catheters cause infections, bacteraemia, discomfort, delirium and immobility; two catheter-source bacteraemias occurred last year. Nurses are unsure whether they may remove catheters without an order.
response.currentPractice: Removal depends on a physician order; indications are often undocumented; catheter days are recorded in flowsheets in three hospitals and on paper in Hospital D.
response.whyNow: Council approval is in place, a Lean coach is available for one hospital at a time, and the point count showed a high share of catheters without an indication.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Patients have a urinary catheter only while it is needed, and no patient has a catheter reinserted because it was removed without a plan.
response.summary: Problem framed as a multi-site Lean project on catheter duration, with infections as a descriptive safety outcome.

records.title: Nurse-driven catheter removal protocols and catheter utilisation: a multi-hospital interrupted time series
records.authors: Okoro-Lindahl B, Castellanos-Pike R, Mensah-Vogel T
records.abstract: Across 9 hospitals, a nurse-driven removal protocol with daily catheter review was introduced in a staggered sequence over 18 months. Catheter utilisation fell from 21 to 14 catheter days per 100 patient days, and segmented regression showed a level change at introduction in 7 of 9 hospitals. The infection rate per 1,000 catheter days did not change clearly (2.1 before and 1.9 after), and the number of infections was too small to estimate an effect with precision. Reinsertion within 48 hours of removal followed 4 percent of removals, similar before and after. Hospitals with a named ward champion sustained the change for longer.

records.title: Value stream mapping of the urinary catheter pathway from emergency department to ward
records.abstract: In one hospital, a team mapped the catheter pathway from insertion in the emergency department to removal on the ward, timing each step for 40 patients. Catheters inserted in the emergency department had no documented indication in 45 percent of cases, and the median wait between the first day a catheter was no longer needed and its removal was 2.5 days. Most of the wait arose at handoffs between teams, where no one owned the removal decision. After standard work and a daily huddle check, the median wait fell to 1 day in a second mapping of 40 patients. The study had no comparison group.

records.title: Interventions to reduce catheter-associated urinary tract infection: a systematic review of controlled and time-series studies
records.authors: Rahman-Keller S, Oduya-Brandt L, Petrakis-Hughes M, Sato-Obi N
records.abstract: We included 31 studies of reminders, stop orders, nurse-driven removal and bundles. Catheter use fell in most studies, with a median relative reduction of 32 percent. Only 8 studies reported infection rates with enough events to estimate change, and their pooled rate ratio was 0.69 (95 percent CI 0.52 to 0.91), with high heterogeneity. Most studies were uncontrolled before-and-after designs at high risk of bias. Studies using interrupted time series with at least eight points before and after were less likely to report large effects.

records.title: Measuring catheter days when electronic flowsheets are incomplete: agreement between point prevalence counts and daily records
records.abstract: On 14 wards we compared catheter days from electronic flowsheets with estimates from twice-weekly point prevalence counts. Estimates from the counts agreed with the flowsheet within 8 percent over a month, but weekly estimates varied more, and short catheterisations under two days were missed by the counts. Wards using paper records could produce monthly utilisation from the counts with about 3 hours of staff time a month. The authors advise against mixing the two sources within one ward's time series, because a switch of source can look like a change in practice.

records.title: Staggered rollout of improvement work across hospitals: designing for inference with multiple baselines
records.authors: Lindgren-Oyelowo E, Tanaka-Ferreira J, Brennan-Quist H
records.abstract: We describe how to plan improvement work that starts at different times in different hospitals so that each hospital acts as a control for the others while it waits. With four sites and three-month intervals, each site contributes a different baseline length, and a segmented regression with site-specific levels can separate the change at each start from secular trends. Simulations with 12 monthly points before the first start showed that staggered starts detected a 25 percent level change with 80 percent power where simultaneous starts reached 55 percent. Autocorrelation and seasonal infection patterns must be modelled explicitly.

records.title: Catheter reinsertion after nurse-driven removal: a balancing measure
records.abstract: Across 6 wards, 1,240 catheter removals under a nurse-driven protocol were followed for 72 hours. Reinsertion occurred after 5.2 percent of removals, most often for urinary retention in men over 75 after surgery. A bladder scan before any reinsertion reduced unnecessary reinsertions over the following year. The authors recommend reporting reinsertion within 72 hours as a balancing measure with any removal protocol, and describing retention episodes separately so that a rise in reinsertions is not hidden inside falling catheter days.

records.title: Why catheters stay: ward nurses on removal decisions
records.authors: Nakashima-Ortiz P, Adeleke-Svensson M, Reid-Castaneda A
records.abstract: We talked with 28 ward nurses in three hospitals about decisions to remove urinary catheters. Nurses described uncertainty about whether they were allowed to remove a catheter without a physician order, fear of reinsertion if the patient could not void, and handoffs where the reason for the catheter was lost. Several described catheters left in to manage incontinence or falls risk at night. Nurses on wards with a written removal protocol described fewer delays and more confidence in raising removal at the morning huddle.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Nurse-driven removal with daily review is consistently followed by fewer catheter days (21 to 14 per 100 patient days across 9 hospitals), while infection effects are imprecise and larger in weaker designs. Value stream mapping located most removal delay at handoffs. A staggered start across four sites gives far more power than a simultaneous start. Point counts can measure catheter days on paper-record wards if the source is not mixed within a series. Reinsertion after removal is about 5 percent and should be tracked. Nurses need explicit authority to remove catheters.
response.gradeRationale: Time-series and before-and-after studies with consistent reductions in catheter use but imprecise and heterogeneous infection effects; a simulation-based methods paper and small qualitative work.
response.summary: Seven records appraised; six source-derived claims; overall certainty low.

response.reading: Catheter duration is set by a chain of handoffs from the inserting team to the ward, where the indication is often lost and no one owns removal. Standard work at the ward (nurse-driven removal, huddle check, flowsheet reminder) acts at the point where waits accumulate. The single Lean coach forces a staggered start, which is also the design that gives the most power to separate change from secular trends. Hospital D's paper records and pending information governance agreement shape how its data can be measured and shared. Infections are the outcome patients care about most but are too few on 12 wards to show change.

response.rationale: The goal is to remove waste from a care pathway across four hospitals, which is what value stream mapping and standard work are for. The single coach makes a staggered start unavoidable, and the retrieved methods paper shows that a staggered multiple-baseline layout gives far more power than a simultaneous start (c4). Catheter days per 100 patient days is responsive (c1); infections are too few to test (c2). Reporting follows SQUIRE 2.0.

response.whyNotMoreComplex: Randomising the order would add little because the coach's availability already fixes it, and a trial would promise an infection effect these wards cannot show.

response.designSummary: Interrupted time series with a common start in February 2027: 12 monthly baseline points and 14 monthly intervention points per ward, pooled across 12 wards.
response.sampleSize: Twelve wards with 26 monthly points each give 312 ward-months. With a baseline near 19 catheter days per 100 patient days and ward-to-ward variation of about 4, a pooled segmented regression can detect a level change of about 20 percent with 80 percent power, assuming modest autocorrelation; infections (about 2 per 1,000 catheter days) are too few for any test.
response.primaryAnalysis: Segmented Poisson regression of monthly catheter days with patient days as the offset, a common change point in February 2027, ward random effects and a first-order autoregressive term.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Descriptive infection rates; run charts of indication documentation and reinsertion.
response.missingData: Months with incomplete flowsheet extracts are flagged and excluded from the model; no imputation.
response.multiplicity: One primary measure; secondary and balancing measures are descriptive.
response.software: R; code archived before the first start.
response.summary: Pooled segmented regression with one common change point.

response.risks: Low: the project changes who removes catheters and when. The main risks are unsafe removal leading to retention and reinsertion, and staff feeling blamed for catheters left in; results are reported by ward, never by nurse.
response.consent: Standard work is usual care under an approved nurse-driven protocol; patients are told why their catheter is being removed and can ask to keep it pending review. Staff take part as part of normal work.
response.data: Ward-level counts only leave each hospital; patient identifiers stay in the local surveillance system; Hospital D's data are shared only after its information governance office agrees.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: older men after surgery bear most reinsertion risk, patients with dementia or limited English may not report retention symptoms, and night-shift wards have fewer staff to act on reminders. Reinsertion is reported by age group, bladder scanning is used before reinsertion, and interpreters are used for removal explanations.
response.effectiveness: Success is a sustained fall in catheter days with reinsertion below 6 percent; infections are described, never claimed as an effect.
response.efficiency: Existing staff, one coach and existing data systems.
response.costs: Staff time within normal work; bladder scanners already on the wards.
response.grants: None needed; a regional spread grant could follow.
response.partnerships: Four ward manager champions, the regional Lean office, urology and emergency leads, and two patient partners from the regional advisory council.
response.rebPath: Screened by the regional research ethics office as quality improvement not requiring REB review (QI-R-2026-077); any later publication follows SQUIRE 2.0.

response.designSummary: Multiple-baseline interrupted time series with staggered starts: Hospital A in January, B in April, C in July and D in October 2027; monthly catheter days per ward from each hospital's baseline to March 2028.
response.sampleSize: Twelve wards contribute about 300 ward-months. With four hospitals starting at three-month intervals and at least 11 baseline months each, the retrieved simulation shows about 80 percent power to detect a 25 percent level change, against about 55 percent for a simultaneous start (c4). With a baseline near 19 catheter days per 100 patient days, a 25 percent change is a fall to about 14, similar to the published multi-hospital result (c1). Infections, at about 2 per 1,000 catheter days, give too few events for any test and are described only.
response.primaryAnalysis: Segmented Poisson regression of monthly catheter days with patient days as the offset, hospital-specific change points at each start, hospital-specific levels (so Hospital D's point-count series has its own level), ward random effects, calendar month terms for seasonality and a first-order autoregressive error. The main estimate is the average level change across hospitals; the concurrent comparison with hospitals not yet started is shown alongside.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Sensitivity analysis excluding Hospital D; descriptive infection rates per 1,000 catheter days; run charts of indication documentation and reinsertion by age group.
response.missingData: Months with incomplete flowsheet extracts or missed point counts are flagged and excluded, never imputed; Hospital D's data enter the pooled model only after its information governance agreement.
response.multiplicity: One primary estimate; secondary and balancing measures are descriptive.
response.software: R; model code and change points archived before Hospital A starts.
overfittingGuards: Change points fixed by the coach schedule before any data are seen
Hospital D's series never switches measurement source
response.summary: Staggered multiple-baseline analysis with hospital-specific change points; about 80 percent power for a 25 percent level change.

items.theme: Nobody knew why it was there
items.quote: Composite paraphrase: I kept asking why I still had the tube, and every nurse said the doctor would decide.
items.implication: Nurse-driven removal needs visible authority at the bedside and a documented indication.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase: If I take it out at night and he cannot pass urine, I am the one putting a new one in at four in the morning.
items.implication: Pair removal with a bladder scan rule and report reinsertion as a balancing measure.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase: They arrive from theatre with a catheter and no plan, and after two shift changes nobody remembers why.
items.implication: Map the theatre handoff first and add the indication to the transfer note.

items.quote: Composite paraphrase: They left it in because Mum was wet at night, but she hated it and it made her confused.
items.implication: Address incontinence care as part of standard work, not as a reason to keep a catheter.

response.summary: Four composite voices on authority, reinsertion, theatre handoffs and incontinence.

response.title: A staggered Lean project to shorten urinary catheter duration on 12 wards in four hospitals
response.abstract: Problem: urinary catheters stayed longer than needed on 12 wards in four hospitals. Intervention: value stream mapping and standard work (nurse-driven removal, huddle check, removal reminder), introduced one hospital per quarter as the Lean coach moved. Measures: monthly catheter days per 100 patient days (primary), infections (descriptive), indication documentation (process) and reinsertion within 72 hours (balancing). Results will be written after March 2028.
response.introduction: Catheter duration is driven by handoffs where the indication is lost. Nurse-driven removal reduces catheter days in multi-hospital series, while infection effects are imprecise.
response.methods: Multiple-baseline interrupted time series with hospital-specific change points and hospital-specific levels; Hospital D used point counts for its whole series. The project was screened as quality improvement.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will show each hospital's series with its start marked, the pooled level change, infections, documentation and reinsertion.
response.discussion: The discussion will separate the level change at each start from regional trends using the hospitals not yet started. It will report infections descriptively and will not claim an infection effect.
response.limitations: The order of hospitals was fixed by coach availability, not randomised. Hospital D used a different measurement source, and infections were too few to test.
response.conclusion: To be written after the final hospital's six-month follow-up. It will state whether catheter days fell at each start and whether reinsertion stayed within its threshold.
response.summary: SQUIRE draft for the staggered project; results empty until data exist.
